content: Healthcare facilities that care for patients with suspected or confirmed MERS-CoV infection must implement stringent measures to minimize the risk of virus transmission to other patients, healthcare workers, and visitors. Infection control guidelines for both home-care settings and healthcare facilities are available on the WHO coronavirus infections webpage. It is essential to provide regular education and training on infection prevention and control to all healthcare workers. Rabies is a preventable viral zoonotic disease, but it is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. It causes approximately 55,000 deaths globally each year, with children being the primary victims. Post-exposure vaccination is highly effective in preventing the disease and is estimated to avert an additional 327,000 rabies deaths annually. Despite advancements in rabies control measures, the incidence of rabies in Asia has not significantly decreased, except in a few island nations. Over 95% of human rabies deaths occur in Asia and Africa, with the virus primarily maintained in dogs (urban rabies) and wild animals (sylvatic rabies). Human rabies cases are predominantly caused by bites from rabid dogs, accounting for 94% of cases, while transmission from other wild carnivores is rare. Rabies is transmitted through bites or scratches from infected animals, contact with infectious saliva on mucosa or open wounds, or organ transplantation (e.g., cornea). The incubation period is typically 4–8 weeks but can extend to years. Once clinical symptoms develop, the disease is almost always fatal. Symptoms progress in phases, starting with pain or tingling at the bite site, hydrophobia, restlessness, excessive salivation, convulsions, and ultimately death. Immediate post-bite treatment, including vaccination and rabies immunoglobulin, is highly effective in preventing the disease. However, there is no cure once symptoms appear. Pre-exposure vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups, such as children, veterinarians, and dog handlers. Community-level mass vaccination of dogs, achieving over 80% coverage, effectively eliminates human rabies cases. Public awareness, dog population management, and proper waste management are also critical. Internationally, the movement of unvaccinated dogs is restricted to prevent rabies spread. World Rabies Day, observed on September 29, raises awareness about rabies prevention and control. Rift Valley Fever (RVF) outbreaks in animals often manifest as mass mortality among young animals or waves of unexplained abortions in livestock. These outbreaks typically precede human cases, particularly among individuals working with animals. Heavy rains often trigger outbreaks. The overall case-fatality rate in humans is less than 1%, but post-infection complications can have severe socioeconomic and health impacts. RVF is caused by the Phlebovirus, a member of the Bunyaviridae family, and is primarily transmitted through infected livestock and mosquito vectors. Human infection risk is low in the South-East Asia Region but could increase due to the illegal import of infected animals. Occupational groups such as veterinarians, animal handlers, and slaughterhouse workers are at higher risk. Transmission occurs through mosquito bites, contact with infected animal tissues or fluids, or inhalation of aerosols during slaughter. The incubation period is about one week, and most human cases are mild, presenting flu-like symptoms. Severe cases may involve ocular, meningoencephalitis, or hemorrhagic syndromes, with fatalities primarily occurring in hemorrhagic cases. There is no vaccine or specific treatment for humans; supportive therapy is the only option for severe cases. Prevention includes careful handling of diseased animals, public awareness, and restricting livestock trade from infected areas. Viral hepatitis is an infectious disease causing liver inflammation, often presenting as jaundice, loss of appetite, nausea, fatigue, and abdominal discomfort. There are five types of hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, D, and E), each with distinct transmission routes. Hepatitis A and E are foodborne and waterborne, causing acute illness, while hepatitis B, C, and D are transmitted through infected blood, medical equipment, sexual contact, or mother-to-child transmission. Hepatitis B and C are major public health concerns due to their potential to cause chronic liver damage, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Approximately 70–80% of cirrhosis and liver cancer cases are linked to hepatitis B and C. Co-infection with HIV accelerates liver disease progression. Hepatitis E outbreaks are common in the South-East Asia Region, with over 50% of global deaths from hepatitis E occurring there. Prevention strategies vary based on transmission mode and include vaccination, safe water, hygiene, and public education. Vaccines for hepatitis A and B are available, with hepatitis B vaccination included in universal immunization programs in many countries.
